title: Theory of computation
audience: a college student in a mathematics degree program (or a related major such as physics, computer science or economics), or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study what computers can and cannot do: finite automata and regular languages, regular expressions, the pumping lemma, context-free grammars and pushdown automata, Turing machines and the Church–Turing thesis, decidability, the halting problem and reductions, and the complexity classes P and NP.
primary_reading: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.404J: Theory of Computation (free lectures)

weeks.2: NFAs and their equivalence with DFAs
weeks.4: The pumping lemma and non-regular languages

blocks.deliverable: Design five DFAs and convert an NFA to a DFA.
Prove two languages are not regular.
Week 7 midterm; design a Turing machine and trace it.
Prove a problem undecidable by reduction.
Show a problem is in NP and sketch a reduction.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Write simulators in Python for DFAs, NFAs and Turing machines, use them to test machines you design for supplied languages, and write proofs that two of the languages are non-regular or undecidable.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
